To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

we conducted an electronic health record based phenome wide association study to explore pleiotropic associations of variants in FTO, some of which have previously been associated with obesity and T2D, and found that FTO variants are associated with sleep apnoea, fibrocystic disease of the breast, and non-alcoholic liver diseases, among others, and that these associations were attenuated after adjusting for obesity, suggesting that some of these associations are not mediated by BMI.

we performed PheWAS using EHR data to explore pleiotropic associations with genetic variants in Fto and identified novel associations with obesity-associated variants as well as associations between variants not associated with BMI with other phenotypes.
FTO genetic variation is pleiotropic and some associations may be mediated through BMI.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the pleiotropic nature of the FTO locus and the potential for EHR-based PheWAS studies to identify novel associations.

pleiotropy of obesity-associated FTO genetic variants is not supported by the current data.

FTO is pleiotropic, and that the obesity associated variants have pleiotropy that is at least partially mediated by obesity, while the non-obesity associated variants have pleitropy that is independent of obesity.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
FTO is pleiotropic and the associations are likely to be mediated by BMI, except for the association with sleep apnea, which is likely to be independent of BMI.
the FTO gene is a complex gene that is involved in a wide range of phenotypes, some of which may not be mediated by body mass index.
FTO variants are associated with a broad spectrum of phenotypes, some of which may be independent of the well-described associations of FTO variants and BMI.
The main takeaway from our work is that
pleiotropy of FTO variants may be more complex than previously appreciated.
PheWAS can help identify potential pleiotropy of variants in FTO and other genes, which may help to identify novel therapeutic targets for disease.
PheWAS is an important tool for identifying novel genetic associations, but it is also a tool that can be used to validate previously identified genetic associations.
